claim: KSR1 serves as a scaffold for Raf, MEK, and ERK enabling the efficient transmission of signals within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade.
source: Kinase Suppressor of Ras 1 (KSR1) serves as a scaffold for Raf, MEK, and ERK enabling the efficient transmission of signals within the mitogen activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade (Kortum and Lewis, 2004; Nguyen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kortum and Lewis, 2004; Nguyen et al., 2002).

claim: KSR1 is dispensable for normal development.
source: Although KSR1 is dispensable for normal development, it is necessary for oncogenic Ras-induced tumorigenesis including colorectal cancer cells (Kortum and Lewis, 2004; Nguyen et al., 2002; Fisher et al., 2011; Fisher et al., 2015; Morrison et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: KSR1 is necessary for oncogenic Ras-induced tumorigenesis including colorectal cancer cells.
source: Although KSR1 is dispensable for normal development, it is necessary for oncogenic Ras-induced tumorigenesis including colorectal cancer cells (Kortum and Lewis, 2004; Nguyen et al., 2002; Fisher et al., 2011; Fisher et al., 2015; Morrison et al., 2009; Rao et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Activating Ras mutations are present in over 40% of colorectal cancers (CRC).
source: Activating Ras mutations are present in over 40 % of colorectal cancers (CRC), and associated with advanced disease and decreased overall survival (Haigis, 2017; Serebriiskii et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Haigis, 2017; Serebriiskii et al., 2019).

claim: Activating Ras mutations are associated with advanced disease and decreased overall survival.
source: Activating Ras mutations are present in over 40 % of colorectal cancers (CRC), and associated with advanced disease and decreased overall survival (Haigis, 2017; Serebriiskii et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Haigis, 2017; Serebriiskii et al., 2019).

claim: Raf/MEK/ERK signaling can phenocopy Ras signaling essential for CRC growth and survival.
source: Raf/MEK/ERK signaling can phenocopy Ras signaling essential for CRC growth and survival (Schmitz et al., 2007; Brandt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Schmitz et al., 2007; Brandt et al., 2019).

claim: Oncogene-driven signaling pathways promote mRNA translation that enables expression of a subset of mRNAs to promote growth, invasion, and metastasis.
source: Oncogene-driven signaling pathways promote mRNA translation that enables expression of a subset of mRNAs to promote growth, invasion, and metastasis (Chu et al., 2016; Avdulov et al., 2004; Truitt Morgan et al., 2015; Pelletier et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Tumor cells have an increased dependence on cap-dependent translation, unlike their normal complements.
source: Tumor cells have an increased dependence on cap-dependent translation, unlike their normal complements (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015; Truitt and Ruggero, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015; Truitt and Ruggero, 2016).

claim: Eukaryotic Translation Initiation Factor 4E (eIF4E) is a rate-limiting factor for oncogenic transformation.
source: Eukaryotic Translation Initiation Factor 4E (eIF4E) is a rate-limiting factor for oncogenic transformation, with reductions of as little as 40 % being sufficient to block tumorigenesis (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).

claim: Reductions of eIF4E of as little as 40% are sufficient to block tumorigenesis.
source: Eukaryotic Translation Initiation Factor 4E (eIF4E) is a rate-limiting factor for oncogenic transformation, with reductions of as little as 40 % being sufficient to block tumorigenesis (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).

claim: Disruption of KSR1 or ERK inhibition leads to dephosphorylation and activation of 4EBP1.
source: Importantly, disruption of KSR1 or ERK inhibition leads to dephosphorylation and activation of 4EBP1, indicating that the function of KSR1 as an ERK scaffold is key to the aberrant regulation of mRNA translation (McCall et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (McCall et al., 2016).

claim: The function of KSR1 as an ERK scaffold is key to the aberrant regulation of mRNA translation.
source: Importantly, disruption of KSR1 or ERK inhibition leads to dephosphorylation and activation of 4EBP1, indicating that the function of KSR1 as an ERK scaffold is key to the aberrant regulation of mRNA translation (McCall et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (McCall et al., 2016) and logical inference from the preceding statement.

claim: KSR1-dependent regulation of mRNA translation of a subset of genes was predicted to selectively promote survival of CRC cells but not normal colon epithelia.
source: This tumor-specific, KSR1-dependent regulation of mRNA translation of a subset of genes was predicted to selectively promote survival of CRC cells but not normal colon epithelia (McCall et al., 2016; Neilsen et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (McCall et al., 2016; Neilsen et al., 2019).

claim: Almost all CRC originates from epithelial cells lining the colon or rectum of the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Almost all CRC originates from epithelial cells lining the colon or rectum of the gastrointestinal tract, but in order to invade to the surrounding tissue, cancer cells lose cell adhesiveness to acquire motility and become invasive, characterized by the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), which is central to tumor pathogenesis (Ye and Weinberg, 2015; Nieto, 2013; Thiery et al., 2009; Dongre and Weinberg, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EMT is central to tumor pathogenesis.
source: Almost all CRC originates from epithelial cells lining the colon or rectum of the gastrointestinal tract, but in order to invade to the surrounding tissue, cancer cells lose cell adhesiveness to acquire motility and become invasive, characterized by the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), which is central to tumor pathogenesis (Ye and Weinberg, 2015; Nieto, 2013; Thiery et al., 2009; Dongre and Weinberg, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EMT involves a complex cellular process during which epithelial cells lose polarity, cell-cell contacts and acquire mesenchymal characteristics.
source: EMT involves a complex cellular process during which epithelial cells lose polarity, cell-cell contacts and acquire mesenchymal characteristics.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about EMT.

claim: EMT is crucial for cell plasticity during embryonic development, trans differentiation and wound healing.
source: While EMT is crucial for cell plasticity during embryonic development, trans differentiation and wound healing, when aberrantly activated EMT has deleterious effects, which facilitate motility and invasion of cancer cells (Nieto, 2013; Thiery et al., 2009; Dongre and Weinberg, 2019; Nieto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When aberrantly activated, EMT has deleterious effects, which facilitate motility and invasion of cancer cells.
source: While EMT is crucial for cell plasticity during embryonic development, trans differentiation and wound healing, when aberrantly activated EMT has deleterious effects, which facilitate motility and invasion of cancer cells (Nieto, 2013; Thiery et al., 2009; Dongre and Weinberg, 2019; Nieto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EMT has been shown to be controlled by transcription-dependent mechanisms, especially through repression of genes that are hallmarks of epithelial phenotype such as E-cadherin.
source: EMT has been shown to be controlled by transcription-dependent mechanisms, especially through repression of genes that are hallmarks of epithelial phenotype such as E-cadherin.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about EMT mechanisms.

claim: Loss of E-cadherin at the membrane has been associated with carcinoma progression and EMT.
source: Loss of E-cadherin at the membrane has been associated with carcinoma progression and EMT (Thiery et al., 2009; Thiery, 2002; Oda et al., 1994; Frixen et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: E-cadherin function is transcriptionally repressed through the action of EMT transcription factors (TFs), including Snail-family proteins (Snail1, Slug), zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 and 2 (ZEB1 and ZEB2), and twist-related protein (Twist).
source: E-cadherin function is transcriptionally repressed through the action of EMT transcription factors (TFs), including Snail-family proteins (Snail1, Slug), zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 and 2 (ZEB1 and ZEB2), and twist-related protein (Twist) (Nieto et al., 2016; Jolly et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Nieto et al., 2016; Jolly et al., 2017).

claim: Inappropriate induction of non-epithelial cadherins, such as N-cadherin by epithelial cells are known to play a fundamental role during initiation of metastasis.
source: Inappropriate induction of non-epithelial cadherins, such as N-cadherin by epithelial cells are known to play a fundamental role during initiation of metastasis (Nieman et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2017; Suyama et al., 2002; Rosivatz et al., 2004; Okubo et al., 2017; Sadot et al., 1998; Loh et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: N-cadherin disassembles adherent junction complexes, disrupting the intercellular cohesion and reorienting the migration of cells, away from the direction of cell-cell contact.
source: N-cadherin disassembles adherent junction complexes, disrupting the intercellular cohesion and reorienting the migration of cells, away from the direction of cell-cell contact (Nieman et al., 1999; Scarpa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Nieman et al., 1999; Scarpa et al., 2015).

claim: Upregulation of N-cadherin expression promotes motility and invasion.
source: Upregulation of N-cadherin expression promotes motility and invasion (Nieman et al., 1999; Liu et al., 2017; Suyama et al., 2002; Hulit et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Central to the process of EMT is the coordinated loss of E-cadherin expression and the upregulation of N-cadherin gene expression, termed cadherin switching.
source: Thus, central to the process of EMT is the coordinated loss of E-cadherin expression and the upregulation of N-cadherin gene expression, termed cadherin switching (Loh et al., 2019; Wheelock et al., 2008; Tomita et al., 2000; Maeda et al., 2005; Araki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated transcriptional regulation of EMT through oncogenic Ras or its downstream effector signaling pathways via the activation of EMT-TFs.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated transcriptional regulation of EMT through oncogenic Ras or its downstream effector signaling pathways via the activation of EMT-TFs (Shin et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2019; Andreolas et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2010; Lemieux et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oncogenic Ras itself activates EMT-TF Slug to induce EMT in skin and colon cancer cells.
source: Oncogenic Ras itself activates EMT-TF Slug to induce EMT in skin and colon cancer cells (Wong et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Wong et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2010).

claim: Enhanced activity of ERK2 but not ERK1, has been linked with Ras-dependent regulation of EMT.
source: Enhanced activity of ERK2 but not ERK1, has been linked with Ras-dependent regulation of EMT (Shin et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Shin et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2019).

claim: Several studies have described an alternative program wherein cells lose their epithelial phenotype, via post-transcriptional modifications rather than transcriptional repression involving translational regulation or protein internalization.
source: Several studies have also described an alternative program wherein cells lose their epithelial phenotype, via post-transcriptional modifications rather than transcriptional repression involving translational regulation or protein internalization (Jechlinger et al., 2003; Aiello et al., 2018; Waerner et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Expression profiling of polysome-bound mRNA to assess translational efficiency identified over 30 genes that were translationally regulated upon Ras and TGFβ inducing EMT.
source: Expression profiling of polysome-bound mRNA to assess translational efficiency identified over 30 genes that were translationally regulated upon Ras and TGFβ inducing EMT (Jechlinger et al., 2003; Waerner et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Jechlinger et al., 2003; Waerner et al., 2006).

claim: EPSTI1 was identified as a stromal fibroblast-induced gene upon co-cultures of breast cancer cells with stomal fibroblasts.
source: EPSTI1 was identified as a stromal fibroblast-induced gene upon co-cultures of breast cancer cells with stomal fibroblasts (Nielsen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Nielsen et al., 2002).

claim: EPSTI1 is expressed at low levels in normal breast and colon tissue but aberrantly expressed in breast tumor tissue.
source: EPSTI1 is expressed at low levels in normal breast and colon tissue but aberrantly expressed in breast tumor tissue (Nielsen et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Nielsen et al., 2002).

claim: EPSTI1 promotes cell invasion and malignant growth of primary breast tumor cells.
source: EPSTI1 promotes cell invasion and malignant growth of primary breast tumor cells (Li et al., 2014; de Neergaard et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Li et al., 2014; de Neergaard et al., 2010).

claim: Polysome profiling in CRC cells found that KSR1- and ERK induces EPSTI1 mRNA translation.
source: We performed polysome profiling in CRC cells and found that KSR1- and ERK induces of EPSTI1 mRNA translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from polysome profiling described in the manuscript.

claim: EPSTI1 is both necessary and sufficient for coordinating the upregulation of N-cadherin with the downregulation of E-cadherin to stimulate cell motility and invasion in colon cancer cells.
source: EPSTI1 is both necessary and sufficient for coordinating the upregulation of N-cadherin with the downregulation of E-cadherin to stimulate cell motility and invasion in colon cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing effects of EPSTI1 knockdown and overexpression.

claim: ERK signaling regulates global and selective mRNA translation through RSK1/2-dependent modification of cap-dependent translation.
source: ERK signaling regulates global and selective mRNA translation through RSK1/2-dependent modification of cap-dependent translation (McCall et al., 2016; Roux et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (McCall et al., 2016; Roux et al., 2007).

claim: Phosphorylation of cap binding protein 4E-BP1 releases eIF4E to promote translation.
source: Phosphorylation of cap binding protein 4E-BP1 releases eIF4E to promote translation and the abundance of eIF4E is a rate-limiting factor for oncogenic Ras- and Myc-driven transformation (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).

claim: The abundance of eIF4E is a rate-limiting factor for oncogenic Ras- and Myc-driven transformation.
source: Phosphorylation of cap binding protein 4E-BP1 releases eIF4E to promote translation and the abundance of eIF4E is a rate-limiting factor for oncogenic Ras- and Myc-driven transformation (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Truitt Morgan et al., 2015).

claim: KSR1 maximizes ERK activation in the setting of oncogenic Ras.
source: We showed previously that KSR1 maximizes ERK activation in the setting of oncogenic Ras (Kortum et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors (Kortum et al., 2006).

claim: KSR1 is required for increased Myc translation via dephosphorylation of 4E-BP1, supporting CRC cell growth.
source: We showed previously that KSR1 maximizes ERK activation in the setting of oncogenic Ras (Kortum et al., 2006), which is required for increased Myc translation via dephosphorylation of 4E-BP1, supporting CRC cell growth (McCall et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (McCall et al., 2016).

claim: The ERK scaffold function of KSR1 alters the translational landscape in CRC cells to support their survival.
source: These observations imply that the ERK scaffold function of KSR1 alters the translational landscape in CRC cells to support their survival.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the preceding observations about KSR1's role in ERK signaling and translation regulation.

claim: A significant number of mRNAs showed either reduced TE or upregulated TE upon KSR1 disruption in both HCT116 and HCT15 cells.
source: We used Anota2seq (Oertlin et al., 2019) to calculate translation efficiency (TE) by comparing the differences in efficiently translated mRNAs to the total transcript of each mRNA and observed that a significant number of mRNAs ([selDeltaTP ≥ log (1.2) and selDeltaPT ≥ log (1.2)] and p-value < 0.05) showed either reduced TE or upregulated TE upon KSR1 disruption (Figure 1B, C, Supplementary file 1, Source data 1) in both HCT116 and HCT15 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from polysome profiling and RNA sequencing shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis identified 11 mRNAs in the gene set titled 'Hallmark EMT signature', 'Jechlinger EMT Up', and 'Gotzmann EMT up', that had significantly decreased translation upon KSR1 disruption.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) of significantly enriched genes in HCT116 and HCT15 (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B), identified 11 mRNAs in the gene set titled "Hallmark EMT signature", "Jechlinger EMT Up", and "Gotzmann EMT up" , that had significantly decreased translation upon KSR1 disruption (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: EPSTI1 was one of the highly significant mRNAs with decreased translation among the genes with decreased translation upon KSR1 disruption.
source: Among the genes with decreased translation, EPSTI1 was one of the highly significant mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the GSEA analysis results described in the preceding text.

claim: EPSTI1 protein expression was decreased with the knockdown of KSR1 in HCT116 and HCT15 cells.
source: To confirm that EPSTI1 translation is KSR1-dependent, we observed that, EPSTI1 protein expression was decreased with the knockdown of KSR1 in HCT116 and HCT15 cells (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The total mRNA transcript of EPSTI1 was unchanged upon KSR1 disruption.
source: To confirm that EPSTI1 translation is KSR1-dependent, we observed that, EPSTI1 protein expression was decreased with the knockdown of KSR1 in HCT116 and HCT15 cells (Figure 1D), while the total mRNA transcript was unchanged upon KSR1 disruption (Figure 1E, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E, left panel.

claim: EPSTI1 TE was markedly decreased upon KSR1 depletion.
source: EPSTI1 TE was markedly decreased upon KSR1 depletion (Figure 1E, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1E, right panel.

claim: EPSTI1 mRNA shifted from actively translating high-molecular-weight (MW) polysome fractions to low-MW fractions in KSR1 knockdown cells.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of sucrose-gradient fractions of monosome mRNA and polysome RNA distribution confirmed that EPSTI1 mRNA shifted from actively translating high-molecular-weight (MW) polysome fractions to low-MW fractions in KSR1 knockdown cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis of sucrose gradient fractions shown in Figure 1F.

claim: HPRT1 mRNA was insensitive to KSR1 knockdown in HCT116 and HCT15 cells.
source: In contrast, HPRT1 mRNA was insensitive to KSR1 knockdown in HCT116 and HCT15 cells, and qPCR analysis of HPRT1 mRNA isolated from sucrose gradient fractions of control and KSR1 knockdown cells showed no significant shift between the low-MW and the high-MW fractions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: EPSTI1 has a 6 hr half-life in HCT116 cells.
source: To determine if KSR1 promotes EPSTI1 degradation, we first assessed EPSTI1 turnover in HCT116 cells following treatment with a protein-synthesis inhibitor, cycloheximide (CHX) and observed that EPSTI1 has a 6 hr half-life (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cycloheximide chase experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: EPSTI1 turnover was not sensitive to MG132 treatment in HCT116 cells lacking KSR1 expression.
source: We analyzed EPSTI1 turnover using a combination of proteasome inhibitor, MG132 and CHX in control and CRISPR-targeted KSR1 HCT116 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E). EPSTI1 turnover was not sensitive to MG132 treatment in HCT116 cells lacking KSR1 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: In HCT116 cells, KSR1 does not mediate ubiquitin proteosome system (UPS)-mediated degradation of EPSTI1.
source: Therefore, in HCT116 cells, KSR1 does not mediate ubiquitin proteosome system (UPS)-mediated degradation of EPSTI1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that EPSTI1 turnover was not sensitive to proteasome inhibitor MG132.

claim: EPSTI1 translation is induced by KSR1.
source: These data support our conclusion that EPSTI1 translation is induced by KSR1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing KSR1-dependent changes in EPSTI1 protein levels without changes in mRNA levels or protein degradation.

claim: EPSTI1 protein expression was decreased upon KSR1 depletion in HCT116 and HCT15 cells.
source: EPSTI1 protein expression was decreased upon KSR1 depletion in HCT116 and HCT15 cells and EPSTI1 expression was restored in knockout cells upon expression of a KSR1 transgene (+ KSR1) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EPSTI1 expression was restored in knockout cells upon expression of a KSR1 transgene.
source: EPSTI1 protein expression was decreased upon KSR1 depletion in HCT116 and HCT15 cells and EPSTI1 expression was restored in knockout cells upon expression of a KSR1 transgene (+ KSR1) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Treatment with ERK inhibitor SCH772984 suppressed EPSTI1 protein expression in both CRC cell line HCT116 and tumorigenic patient derived colon organoid engineered with deletion of APC, p53, SMAD4, and K-RasG12D mutation (PDO-11 AKPS).
source: Similar to inhibition of KSR1, treatment with ERK inhibitor SCH772984 (Morris et al., 2013) suppressed EPSTI1 protein expression in both CRC cell line HCT116 and tumorigenic patient derived colon organoid engineered with deletion of APC, p53, SMAD4, and K-RasG12D mutation (PDO-11 AKPS) (Figure 2B; Drost et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B and citations to prior research.

claim: mTOR inhibitor AZD8055 robustly inhibited phosphorylation of mTOR substrate p70 S6 kinase.
source: Though mTOR inhibitor, AZD8055 (Chresta et al., 2010) robustly inhibited phosphorylation of mTOR substrate p70 S6 kinase, its ability to decrease EPSTI1 expression in HCT116 cells was weak relative to treatment with the ERK inhibitor (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ability of mTOR inhibitor AZD8055 to decrease EPSTI1 expression in HCT116 cells was weak relative to treatment with the ERK inhibitor.
source: Though mTOR inhibitor, AZD8055 (Chresta et al., 2010) robustly inhibited phosphorylation of mTOR substrate p70 S6 kinase, its ability to decrease EPSTI1 expression in HCT116 cells was weak relative to treatment with the ERK inhibitor (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ERK affects EPSTI1 expression via mechanisms distinct from mTOR.
source: These observations suggest the ERK affects EPSTI1 expression via mechanisms distinct from mTOR.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects of ERK and mTOR inhibitors on EPSTI1 expression.

claim: The EPSTI1 transcript levels were not altered significantly by SCH772984 treatment in HCT116.
source: While the total protein was reduced upon ERK inhibition in HCT116, the EPSTI1 transcript levels were not altered significantly by SCH772984 treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EPSTI1 mRNA shifted from high-MW fractions to the low-MW fractions upon ERK inhibition.
source: RT-qPCR demonstrated that EPSTI1 mRNA shifted from high-MW fractions to the low-MW fractions upon ERK inhibition (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis of polysome fractions shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The distribution of mRNA for HPRT1 within the same profile was not altered by SCH772984 treatment.
source: The distribution of mRNA for HPRT1 within the same profile was not altered by SCH772984 treatment (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: KSR1-dependent ERK signaling is a critical regulator of EPSTI1 mRNA translation in colon cells and organoids.
source: These data indicate that KSR1-dependent ERK signaling is a critical regulator of EPSTI1 mRNA translation in colon cells and organoids.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing effects of KSR1 disruption and ERK inhibition on EPSTI1 translation.

claim: KSR1 disruption inhibits HCT116 cell anchorage-independent growth in vitro and tumor formation in vivo.
source: KSR1 disruption inhibits HCT116 cell anchorage-independent growth in vitro and tumor formation in vivo (Fisher et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Fisher et al., 2015).

claim: Disruption of KSR1 by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeting decreased HCT116 and HCT15 cell viability under anchorage-independent conditions on simulated by poly-(HEMA) coating.
source: Similarly, disruption of KSR1 by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated targeting decreased HCT116 and HCT15 cell viability under anchorage-independent conditions on simulated by poly-(HEMA) coating (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: KSR1 transgene expression restored cell viability in HCT116 and HCT15 cells lacking KSR1.
source: KSR1 transgene expression restored cell viability in HCT116 and HCT15 cells lacking KSR1 (KSR1 CRISPR+ KSR1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: KSR1 expression is upregulated in colon cancer cell lines when compared to the non-transformed human colon epithelial cells (HCECs).
source: We showed previously that KSR1 expression is upregulated in colon cancer cell lines when compared to the non-transformed human colon epithelial cells (HCECs) (Fisher et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors (Fisher et al., 2015).

claim: EPSTI1 protein is aberrantly expressed in colon cancer cell lines HCT116 and HCT15, while its expression is detected weakly in HCECs.
source: We observed that EPSTI1 protein is aberrantly expressed in colon cancer cell lines HCT116 and HCT15, while its expression is detected weakly in HCECs (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: EPSTI1 protein expression is markedly higher in AKPS organoids than normal colon organoids.
source: EPSTI1 protein expression is also markedly higher in AKPS organoids than normal colon organoids (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: EPSTI1 disruption suppressed viability on poly-(HEMA) coated by 40% in HCT15 cells, and over 70%, in HCT116 cells.
source: EPSTI1 disruption suppressed viability on poly-(HEMA) coated by 40 % in HCT15 cells, and over 70%, in HCT116 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: EPSTI1 knockdown reduced colony formation in soft agar by 63% in HCT116 cells and 71% in SW480 cells.
source: EPSTI1 knockdown reduced colony formation in soft agar by 63 % in HCT116 cells and 71 % in SW480 cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: KSR1-dependent translation of ESPTI1 is required for anchorage-independent growth of colon tumor cell lines.
source: These observations show that KSR1-dependent translation of ESPTI1 is required for anchorage-independent growth of colon tumor cell lines.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing effects of KSR1 and EPSTI1 disruption on anchorage-independent growth.

claim: Cells lacking either EPSTI1 or KSR1 were approximately 20% less motile compared to control cells.
source: Cells lacking either EPSTI1 or KSR1 were approximately 20 % less motile compared to control cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch wound assay data described in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Reintroduction of KSR1 expression in CRISPR-targeted HCT116 cells restored motility comparable to the control cells.
source: Reintroduction of KSR1 expression in CRISPR-targeted HCT116 cells restored motility comparable to the control cells (Figure 4A, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by scratch wound assay data shown in Figure 4A, top.

claim: EPSTI1 RNAi suppresses cell invasion through Matrigel by 72% in HCT116 and by 75% in SW480.
source: EPSTI1 RNAi suppresses cell invasion through Matrigel by 72 % in HCT116 and by 75 % in SW480. (Figure 4B, top right and bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by Transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: KSR1 depletion suppressed invasion by 64% in HCT116 and by 53% SW480 cells.
source: KSR1 depletion suppressed invasion by 64 % in HCT116 and by 53 % SW480 cells (Figure 4B, top left and bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by Transwell invasion assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: KSR1-dependent EPSTI1 signaling contributes to cell migration and invasion in CRC cells.
source: Overall, these results suggest the KSR1-dependent EPSTI1 signaling contributes to cell migration and invasion in CRC cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing effects of KSR1 and EPSTI1 disruption on cell migration and invasion.

claim: KSR1 disruption in HCT116, HCT15 and SW480 cells had elevated levels of E-cadherin, along with a coincident decrease in EMT-TF Slug.
source: Compared to the non-targeting control, KSR1 disruption in HCT116, HCT15 and SW480 cells had elevated levels of E-cadherin, along with a coincident decrease in EMT-TF Slug (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of Vimentin, and Snail1 was not changed in HCT116 cells upon KSR1 disruption.
source: Expression of Vimentin, and Snail1 was not changed in HCT116 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upon knockdown of EPSTI1 with either of two siRNA oligos, there was a decrease in the expression of N-cadherin, ZEB1 and Slug.
source: Upon knockdown of EPSTI1 with either of two siRNA oligos, we observed a decrease in the expression of N-cadherin, ZEB1 and Slug.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data described in the text and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Coincident with the decrease in EMT-TFs upon EPSTI1 knockdown, E-cadherin levels were elevated.
source: Coincident with the decrease in EMT-TFs, E-cadherin levels were elevated (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no significant change in the Slug and ZEB1 mRNA upon EPSTI1 knockdown.
source: While there was no significant change in the Slug and ZEB1 mRNA upon EPSTI1 knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: EPSTI1 disruption decreased N-cadherin mRNA expression over 50% in HCT116 and SW480 cells.

claim: The expression of N-cadherin in cells lacking EPSTI1 was sufficient to restore invasiveness to HCT116 cells.

claim: Upregulation of N-cadherin expression enhances motility in multiple cancer cell lines.

claim: Exogenous expression of EPSTI1 in cells lacking KSR1 restored the cadherin switch, by decreasing the expression of E-cadherin and increasing N-cadherin levels comparable to control cells.

claim: Suppression of E-cadherin and restoration of N-cadherin expression by the EPSTI1 transgene reestablished the ability of KSR1 knockout cells to migrate in monolayer culture.

claim: Forced expression of EPSTI1 in KSR1 knockout cells increased the number of invading cells by over threefold.

claim: Over 3 days, EPSTI1 knockdown had no effect on cell proliferation compared to control HCT116 and SW480 cells.
source: Over 3 days, EPSTI1 knockdown had no effect on cell proliferation compared to control HCT116 and SW480 cells.

claim: EPSTI1 expression in KSR1 knockout cells had no significant effect on cell proliferation for 24 hr in HCT116 and SW480 cells.

claim: EPSTI1 expression increased the number of invading cells in 24 hours over 50% in HCT116 and over 70% in SW480 cells.

claim: EPSTI1 expression has a significant effect on cell proliferation over 7 days compared to KSR1 knockout cells in HCT116 and SW480 cells.

claim: EPSTI1 expression rescued migratory potential by over 60% in KSR1-depleted HCT116 and SW480 cells within 24 hr.
source: EPSTI1 expression rescued migratory potential by over 60 % in KSR1-depleted HCT116 and SW480 cells within 24 hr (Figure 6C).

claim: Disabling the cadherin switch and inhibition of cell invasion by KSR1 disruption interrupts EPSTI1 translation.
source: These data reveal that disabling the cadherin switch and inhibition of cell invasion by KSR1 disruption interrupts EPSTI1 translation, highlighting the pivotal role of this pathway for the induction of EMT-like phenotype in CRC cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing effects of KSR1 disruption on EPSTI1 translation and EMT-related phenotypes.

claim: The KSR1-EPSTI1 pathway plays a pivotal role for the induction of EMT-like phenotype in CRC cells.
source: These data reveal that disabling the cadherin switch and inhibition of cell invasion by KSR1 disruption interrupts EPSTI1 translation, highlighting the pivotal role of this pathway for the induction of EMT-like phenotype in CRC cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing effects of KSR1 and EPSTI1 on EMT-related phenotypes.

claim: Upon KSR1 depletion, N-cadherin mRNA decreased 32% in HCT116 and 89% in SW480 cells.
source: Upon KSR1 depletion, N-cadherin mRNA decreased 32 % in HCT116% and 89% in SW480 cells (Figure 7A).

claim: Ectopic expression of EPSTI1 in KSR1 knockout cells restored the N-cadherin mRNA expression to levels observed in control SW480 cells.

claim: In HCT116 KSR1 KO, forced EPSTI1 expression increased N-cadherin mRNA levels threefold above that seen in control HCT116 cells.

claim: EPSTI1 alone was sufficient to dramatically induce the expression of N-cadherin and double the invasive activity of HCECs.

claim: EPSTI1 mediates the expression of N-cadherin to promote invasive behavior in non-transformed colon epithelial cells and colon cancer cells.
source: These data indicate that EPSTI1 mediates the expression of N-cadherin to promote invasive behavior in non-transformed colon epithelial cells and colon cancer cells.

claim: The E- to N-cadherin switch promotes cancer cell survival following the loss of cell adhesion to the extracellular matrix.
source: The E- to N-cadherin switch promotes cancer cell survival following the loss of cell adhesion to the extracellular matrix (Derksen et al., 2006; Onder et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Derksen et al., 2006; Onder et al., 2008).

claim: KSR1 promotes CRC cell survival when detached from a solid substrate.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Fisher et al., 2015; McCall et al., 2016).

claim: Compared to control HCT116 and HCT15 cells, viability decreased approximately 75% in cells lacking KSR1 under anchorage-independent conditions.

claim: The number of colonies formed in HCT116 and SW480 cells dramatically decreased by 75% in the absence of KSR1.

claim: Forced expression of EPSTI1 was sufficient to reverse the suppression of colony formation caused by KSR1 disruption to levels observed in control HCT116 and SW480 cells.
source: Forced expression of EPSTI1 was sufficient to reverse the suppression of colony formation caused by KSR1 disruption to levels observed in control HCT116 and SW480 cells (Figure 7D).

claim: Despite the absence of KSR1 to maintain and support cell growth, ectopic EPSTI1 expression was able to maintain anchorage-independent viability in CRC cells.

claim: Multiple studies have established a relationship between oncogenic Ras-mediated ERK signaling and EMT, either through Ras or its downstream effector signaling pathways activating EMT-TFs.
source: Multiple studies have established a relationship between oncogenic Ras-mediated ERK signaling and EMT, either through Ras or its downstream effector signaling pathways activating EMT-TFs (Shin et al., 2010; Andreolas et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2010; Lemieux et al., 2009; Diesch et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Silencing of Erbin, a tumor suppresser known to disrupt KSR1-RAF1 interaction, promoted cell migration and invasion of colon cancer cells.
source: Silencing of Erbin, a tumor suppresser known to disrupt KSR1-RAF1 interaction, promoted cell migration and invasion of colon cancer cells, but did not identify the mechanism on how KSR1-dependent MAPK signaling affected EMT (Stevens et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Stevens et al., 2018).

claim: Mediators of EMT-like phenotype activate cap-dependent translation initiation have been associated with increased aggressiveness and metastases of cancer cells.
source: Mediators of EMT- like phenotype activate cap-dependent translation initiation have been associated with increased aggressiveness and metastases of cancer cells, and we have shown that KSR1 can affect translation initiation (McCall et al., 2016; Jechlinger et al., 2003; Waerner et al., 2006; Prakash et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: KSR1 can affect translation initiation.
source: Mediators of EMT- like phenotype activate cap-dependent translation initiation have been associated with increased aggressiveness and metastases of cancer cells, and we have shown that KSR1 can affect translation initiation (McCall et al., 2016; Jechlinger et al., 2003; Waerner et al., 2006; Prakash et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research including the authors' own work (McCall et al., 2016).

claim: KSR1 promotes the preferential translation of an EMT-related gene, EPSTI1.
source: Our observations establish the novel role of the scaffold protein KSR1 promoting the preferential translation of an EMT-related gene, EPSTI1, and outline a mechanism for KSR1-dependent stimulation of phenotypic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: KSR1 and ERK increase the translational efficiency of EPSTI1 mRNA.
source: Using gene-expression analysis of the polysome-bound mRNA, we discovered KSR1 and ERK increase the translational efficiency of EPSTI1 mRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by polysome profiling and RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EPSTI1 mediates KSR1-dependent motility, invasion, and anchorage-independent growth coincident with its suppression of EMT-TF, Slug, elevating E-cadherin expression.
source: EPSTI1 mediates KSR1-dependent motility, invasion, and anchorage-independent growth coincident with its suppression of EMT-TF, Slug, elevating E-cadherin expression.

claim: EPSTI1 knockdown decreased the expression of N-cadherin mRNA and protein.

claim: In the absence of KSR1, ectopic expression of EPSTI1 was sufficient to suppress E-cadherin expression, stimulate N-cadherin expression and enhance motility and invasive behavior.

evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ectopic EPSTI1 expression induced invasive behavior in non-transformed colon cells.
source: In the absence of KSR1, ectopic expression of EPSTI1 was sufficient to suppress E-cadherin expression, stimulate N-cadherin expression and enhance motility and invasive behavior, this invasive behavior was also induced in non-transformed colon cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing effects of EPSTI1 expression in HCECs.

source: These data demonstrate that a KSR1- and ERK-regulated component is critical to the execution of the transcriptional program that drives interconversion between epithelial and mesenchymal phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data showing effects of KSR1 and ERK on EPSTI1 translation and EMT-related phenotypes.

claim: The association of EPSTI1 with tumor metastatic potential is supported by observations that EPSTI1 is highly upregulated in invasive breast cancer tissues.
source: The association of EPSTI1 with tumor metastatic potential is supported by observations that EPSTI1 is highly upregulated in invasive breast cancer tissues and suggested the role of EPSTI1 in promoting metastasis, tumorsphere formation, and stemness (Nielsen et al., 2002; Li et al., 2014; de Neergaard et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EPSTI1 has a suggested role in promoting metastasis, tumorsphere formation, and stemness.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The association of EPSTI1 induction of invasion in breast cancer cells was attributed to the increased expression of Slug and Twist mRNA and increased expression of fibronectin and α2β1 integrins.

claim: Differential mRNA splicing is implicated in EMT-related processes.

claim: Splicing regulatory factors have been implicated in the motility and invasive behavior of tumor cells.

claim: The invasive property is not completely lost in KSR1/EPSTI1 disruption, which could be attributed to other mesenchymal markers retained in the cells, such as vimentin.
